title: Mastery Challenge: Ancient Egypt
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Ancient Egypt Levels 1–99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from the Nile’s gift to the rediscovery of Egypt: the flood, the black land, hieroglyphs lost and found, Tutankhamun and Egypt’s legacy. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Ancient Egypt Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from the Nile’s yearly flood to the scholars who taught the world to read Egypt again. Level 1 said this story lasted about 3,000 years; now see how much of it you can carry. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Ancient Egypt: mastered
learned: How hieroglyphs were forgotten, and how the Rosetta Stone helped Champollion read them again.
How Carter's team turned Tutankhamun's tomb into science by recording every object.
Who argues that objects like the Rosetta Stone should return to Egypt, and how museums answer.
Where Egypt lives on today, in our calendar, our alphabet and the word paper.

questions.prompt: An Egyptian farmer watches the last floodwater drain off her fields. What happens next in the farming year?

options.label: Shemu begins, and she harvests at once
options.rationale: Harvest comes at the end of the year.

options.label: Akhet begins, and she waits for the flood
options.rationale: The flood has just ended.

options.label: Peret begins, and she plows and sows the wet silt
The dry season begins, and fields are left empty
options.rationale: Wet, fresh silt is ready for planting.

questions.explanation: As the land emerged in Peret, farmers plowed and sowed the soaked, fertile soil.

questions.prompt: Egyptians called the fertile Nile valley Kemet. What did the name mean?

options.label: The black land
The red land
options.rationale: That’s Deshret, the desert.

options.label: The gift of the river
options.rationale: That’s Herodotus’s phrase.

options.label: The upper land
options.rationale: Kemet is about the soil’s color.

questions.explanation: Kemet, “the black land,” was named for the dark silt the flood left behind.

questions.prompt: Researchers want to find hidden spaces inside the Great Pyramid without moving a block. What do they measure?

options.label: The pyramid’s shadow at noon each day
options.rationale: Shadows can’t show what’s inside.

options.label: Muons from cosmic rays passing through stone
The echoes of shouts in the inner passages
options.rationale: Echoes don’t map hidden spaces.

options.label: How warm the outer blocks get in the sun
options.rationale: Heat readings weren’t the method.

questions.explanation: Stone absorbs some muons, so detectors counting them can map empty spaces inside.

questions.prompt: Manetho wrote his history of Egypt in Greek around 300 BCE, and the Rosetta Stone decree also used Greek. Why Greek?

options.label: Greek was the language of the pharaohs of the Old Kingdom
options.rationale: Greek arrived with much later rulers.

options.label: Greek was the only language that could be carved
options.rationale: Hieroglyphs were carved for thousands of years.

options.label: Hieroglyphs had already been forgotten by then
options.rationale: They were used until 394 CE.

options.label: Egypt was ruled by Macedonian Greek kings

questions.explanation: Under the Ptolemies, Egypt’s rulers spoke Greek, so official and learned texts appeared in Greek too.

questions.prompt: What replaced hieroglyphs as Christianity spread in Egypt?

options.label: Latin letters brought by Rome
options.rationale: Egyptians adapted the Greek alphabet.

options.label: An adapted Greek alphabet, used to write Coptic
Arabic script
options.rationale: The Greek-based alphabet came first.

options.label: Demotic, which then lasted into modern times
options.rationale: The new alphabet was Greek-based.

questions.explanation: Egyptians dropped hieroglyphs for an adapted Greek alphabet, the script of Coptic.

questions.prompt: Thomas Young and Jean-François Champollion both worked on hieroglyphs. Which best describes their roles?

options.label: Young found the Rosetta Stone; Champollion translated it
options.rationale: French soldiers found the stone.

options.label: Champollion read Ptolemy’s name; Young cracked the system
options.rationale: It was the other way round.

options.label: Young read Ptolemy’s name; Champollion cracked the system
They worked side by side as a team in Paris
options.rationale: They were rivals.

questions.explanation: Young showed that signs in the name Ptolemy stood for sounds; Champollion worked out the whole mixed system.

questions.prompt: Why do archaeologists value Carter’s excavation of Tutankhamun’s tomb for more than its gold?

options.label: His team numbered and recorded every object over about ten years
He finished emptying the tomb in a single week
options.rationale: It took about ten years.

options.label: He left every object inside the tomb
options.rationale: The objects were cleared and recorded.

options.label: He kept no notes, so the objects speak for themselves
options.rationale: His records fill an archive at Oxford.

questions.explanation: Carter’s team numbered 5,398 objects and recorded them over about a decade; the archive is in Oxford.

questions.prompt: Zahi Hawass argues the Nefertiti bust left Egypt illegally. What does Berlin’s museum point to?

options.label: A purchase from Egypt’s king in 1950
options.rationale: The museum cites a division of finds.

options.label: A gift from Champollion
options.rationale: Champollion died long before 1912.

options.label: An official division of finds in 1913
The 1801 treaty
options.rationale: That’s the British Museum’s case for the Rosetta Stone.

questions.explanation: Berlin says the bust left through an official division of finds overseen by Egypt’s antiquities service.

questions.prompt: Herodotus called Egypt “the gift of the river.” Which popular myth about the pyramids did his writing also help start?

options.label: That aliens built them
options.rationale: The slave myth is the one tied to him.

options.label: That they were built by slaves
That they carried a deadly curse
options.rationale: That legend grew around Tutankhamun’s tomb.

options.label: That Cleopatra ordered them built
options.rationale: They were built long before her.

questions.explanation: Herodotus, misreadings of Exodus and Hollywood films all fed the idea that slaves built the pyramids.

questions.prompt: Ancient Egypt ended as a Roman province in 30 BCE. Which everyday thing still carries a piece of it?

options.label: The seven-day week, invented at Giza
options.rationale: The legacy in this tree is the calendar year.

options.label: The leap day, from Caesar’s Egyptian-based calendar
The metric system, based on the cubit
options.rationale: That’s not an Egyptian legacy.

options.label: Daylight saving time, from the Nile flood
options.rationale: The flood set seasons, not clocks.

questions.explanation: Caesar adopted Egypt’s solar calendar, with an extra day every fourth year, and our calendar grew from it.
